The basics are simple: return a wai with a smile, never touch anyone's head or point your feet at people or Buddha images, cover your shoulders and knees at temples, and never criticise the monarchy, because Thailand's lèse-majesté law carries long prison sentences. Koh Samui adds its own layers to the Buddhist calendar: southern Thai customs, the Hainanese Chinese festivals of Nathon and Maenam, and the Muslim fishing village of Hua Thanon. Most Thais are forgiving of honest mistakes; a smile, a calm voice and a little effort go a long way.

Good to know: customs vary between families and generations, and between Bangkok and the islands. Laws mentioned here are summarised for general information as of November 2026, not legal advice.

The wai and greetings

The wai is the Thai greeting: palms pressed together as if in prayer, raised towards the face with a slight bow of the head. It says hello, thank you, sorry and goodbye.

  • Height matters: the higher the hands and the deeper the bow, the more respect. Hands at chest level with fingertips near the chin is right for most adults; higher for elders and monks.
  • Who wais first: the younger or junior person wais first, and the other returns it. Hotel staff, waiters and shop assistants will often wai you; a smile and a nod, or a small wai, is a polite reply.
  • Don't overdo it: you don't need to wai street vendors, taxi drivers or children. Over-waiing looks odd rather than polite.
  • Handshakes: common in business and with men who deal with foreigners; follow the other person's lead.
  • Names: Thais use first names with the polite title Khun, as in Khun Somchai. Nicknames are normal, even at work.

The monarchy and the law

The Thai monarchy is deeply respected, and the King's portrait is everywhere, from shops to government offices. Section 112 of the Thai Criminal Code, the lèse-majesté law, makes it a crime to defame, insult or threaten the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, with prison sentences of 3–15 years for each offence. The UK government warns that the law can be interpreted broadly, carries a long prison sentence and also covers accusations about members of the royal family, past and present.

  • Don't discuss the monarchy critically in public, in bars or on social media, even jokingly.
  • Stand still when the royal anthem is played, for example before films in cinemas.
  • The national anthem is broadcast in many public places at 08:00 and 18:00; people stop where they are until it ends.
  • Don't deface, step on or throw banknotes and coins, which carry the King's image.
  • Royal birthdays and memorial days are public holidays, with portraits, flags and ceremonies; see the festival table below.

Buddhism and temple etiquette

Around nine in ten Thais are Theravada Buddhists, and temples (wat) are working places of worship as well as sights. On Samui, the Big Buddha, Wat Plai Laem and Wat Khunaram draw the most visitors.

  • Dress: shoulders and knees covered for men and women; no see-through clothes or swimwear. Some temples lend sarongs; carry a scarf or light trousers to be sure.
  • Shoes: take them off before entering any building with a Buddha image, and wherever you see shoes left outside.
  • Feet and posture: sit with your feet tucked behind you or to the side, never pointing at the Buddha or at monks.
  • Buddha images: don't touch, climb or pose disrespectfully with them. Buying Buddha images as decoration and taking them out of Thailand can need an export permit from the Fine Arts Department. [check]
  • Monks: women must not touch a monk or hand anything directly to one; place it on a cloth or table, or give it to a man to pass on. On buses and boats, give monks the seat.
  • Quiet: keep voices low and phones silent; ask before photographing people praying.
  • Donations: a few coins or notes in the donation box are welcome but never compulsory.

Every major temple, its dress code and opening times are on our Koh Samui temples guide, with individual pages for the Big Buddha, Wat Plai Laem and Wat Khunaram.

Spirit houses

Outside almost every home, hotel and shop on Samui stands a small shrine on a post: a spirit house (san phra phum). It gives a home to the guardian spirits of the land, so that they don't trouble the people living there. Owners leave daily offerings: flowers, incense, rice, fruit, sweets and bottles of red soft drink with straws.

  • Don't touch the offerings or the spirit house, and don't use it as a shelf or a photo prop.
  • Walk around it rather than stepping over offerings on the ground.
  • You will often see small offerings on the bows of boats, on trees and on dashboards; the same respect applies.

Samui's cultures

Southern Thai

Samui is part of southern Thailand, and many older islanders speak the southern dialect (Pak Tai), which is faster and shorter than central Thai. Southern food is hotter and more sour, built on fresh turmeric, coconut and seafood: try gaeng som (sour curry) and khua kling (dry curry). Samui's signature dish is wai khua, octopus cooked in coconut milk.

Hainanese Chinese

Many of Samui's merchant families descend from Hainanese traders who arrived from the 19th century and built the coconut trade. Their shrines are the focus of Chinese New Year: the Hainan shrine in Nathon holds the most traditional rites (which have included face-piercing rituals that may not suit children), Maenam's Chinese temple has lion and dragon dances, and the 16 m bronze Guan Yu statue above Hua Thanon draws crowds. Visit with the same respect as a temple, and ask before photographing rituals. See Nathon and the Guan Yu Shrine.

The Muslim village at Hua Thanon

Hua Thanon, on the south-east coast, is Samui's Muslim fishing village, with its mosque built in 1984, painted fishing boats and a morning fish market. When you visit, dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered), ask before photographing people, don't enter the mosque unless invited, and be discreet with alcohol. During Ramadan, avoid eating and drinking in front of people who are fasting. See Hua Thanon, and the island's story in our history of Koh Samui.

Body language and personal space

  • Head and feet: the head is the highest and most respected part of the body, the feet the lowest. Don't touch heads (even ruffling a child's hair), don't reach over someone's head, and don't put your feet on tables or chairs.
  • Pointing: don't point at people with a finger, and never with your foot. Gesture with an open hand instead.
  • Beckoning: call someone over with your palm facing down and fingers waving towards you; the palm-up "come here" gesture is rude.
  • Affection: holding hands is fine, but kissing and cuddling in public make many Thais uncomfortable, especially in villages and temples.
  • Voice: a soft voice signals respect. Loud groups in restaurants or on boats stand out.
  • The Thai smile: a smile can mean happiness, embarrassment, apology or "please don't make this awkward". Read the situation rather than the smile.

Visiting a Thai home

  • Take off your shoes at the door, even if your hosts say you don't need to.
  • Bring a small gift: fruit, sweets or something from your home country. Gifts are often set aside and opened later, not in front of you.
  • Greet the oldest person first, and accept a drink when it is offered.
  • Sit on the floor with your legs folded to the side, not stretched out towards others.
  • Don't step over people sitting on the floor, or over food.
  • Many homes have a family shrine or a portrait of the King in a high place; keep your feet and belongings well away from it.

Sanuk, sabai and mai pen rai

Three ideas explain a lot about daily life on Samui. Sanuk is fun: work, meals and even chores are better when they are enjoyable and shared. Sabai means comfortable and relaxed, and sabai sabai is the island's default speed. Mai pen rai, "never mind", is how Thais let small problems go rather than argue about them. Visitors who adopt a little of all three, and leave rigid timetables at home, tend to have the best time. That patience matters on an island where boats wait for the weather and plans change with the sea.

Language basics

Thai is a tonal language, so the same syllable can mean different things depending on pitch, but people will understand you from context. Men end polite sentences with khrap, women with kha.

EnglishThai (spoken)When to use it
Hello / goodbyeSawasdee khrap / khaAny greeting, with a wai
Thank youKhop khun khrap / khaAll the time
Sorry / excuse meKho thot khrap / khaSqueezing past, small mistakes
Never mind, no problemMai pen raiThe most Thai phrase of all
How much?Tao rai?Markets and taxis
Too expensivePaeng paiBargaining, with a smile
DeliciousAroiCompliment the cook
Not spicy, pleaseMai phetOrdering food
Yes / noChai / mai chaiConfirming
Where is the toilet?Hong nam yoo tee nai?Everywhere
I don't understandMai khao jaiWhen you're lost

Food culture

  • Sharing: Thai meals are shared. Dishes arrive as they are ready and go in the middle; take a little at a time onto your rice.
  • Spoon and fork: hold the spoon in your right hand and use the fork to push food onto it; the fork doesn't go in your mouth. Chopsticks are for noodle soups. Sticky rice is eaten with the fingers of the right hand.
  • Rice first: the word for eating, kin khao, means "eat rice". Leaving a little food shows you were given enough.
  • Who pays: the oldest or most senior person, or whoever invited, usually pays; splitting the bill is common among friends.
  • Street food: point and smile; pad thai and similar dishes cost about 60–80 THB at markets.

Learn to cook it yourself: our Koh Samui cooking class guide compares classes, and the small-group cooking class in a garden kitchen costs 2,000 THB per person. Where to eat: restaurants and markets.

Dress and beach etiquette

  • Beach and pool: swimwear is fine. Topless sunbathing is not part of Thai culture and is frowned upon, even where nobody stops you.
  • Nudity: public nudity is illegal in Thailand, including on beaches.
  • Away from the sand: put on a shirt and shorts or a dress in shops, restaurants, malls and towns. Riding a scooter shirtless or in a bikini is common among visitors but looks disrespectful to Thais and leaves your skin unprotected in a fall.
  • Government offices, hospitals and immigration: dress neatly: long trousers or a knee-length skirt and a shirt with sleeves. Vests, beachwear and flip-flops look disrespectful at official counters.
  • Social media: the UK government notes that posting images of people drinking alcohol or wearing clothing considered inappropriate can be illegal.

Public indecency can be fined under the Criminal Code. [check]

Saving face, bargaining and tipping

  • Saving face: Thais avoid open confrontation. Raising your voice makes the other person lose face and almost never gets results. Smile, stay calm and explain the problem; if needed, ask a manager quietly.
  • Kreng jai: people may say yes to avoid disappointing you. Ask open questions ("What time does the boat leave?") rather than yes/no ones.
  • Bargaining: normal at markets and with some street vendors, not in shops with price tags, malls, 7-Eleven or restaurants. Start friendly, aim for a fair price, and stop when it's close: a few baht matter more to a vendor than to you.
  • Tipping: not expected but appreciated. Many hotels and restaurants add a 10% service charge (shown as "++" with 7% VAT); otherwise rounding up or leaving small change is normal. Massage therapists, boat crews and guides appreciate a tip for good service.

Muay Thai traditions

Muay Thai, Thai boxing, is a national sport with deep ritual. Before a fight, each boxer performs the wai kru ram muay, a slow dance that honours their teacher and blesses the ring, wearing a sacred headband (mongkol) that is removed by the trainer before the bout. Live music on drums and the Javanese-style oboe follows the rhythm of the fight. In Chaweng, Samui International Muay Thai Stadium holds fights on Tuesday, Friday and Sunday and Phetchbuncha Stadium on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday, from about 21:00; fight-night tickets start at 1,500 THB. Our Muay Thai guide also covers training camps.

Weddings, funerals and merit-making

If you are invited to a Thai ceremony on Samui, a few customs help. At weddings, guests usually give money in an envelope rather than a gift. At funerals, which often last several days at a temple, wear black or white and dress conservatively. Merit-making (tham bun), such as giving food to monks on their morning alms round, is open to visitors: kneel or stand quietly, place the food in the bowl without touching the monk, and don't expect thanks, because the giver gains the merit.

Contested traditions

Some traditions on Samui sit uneasily with visitors. Buffalo fighting, in which two bulls push and lock horns in a ring with heavy betting, has a long history on the island and is exempt from Thailand's animal-cruelty law as a local tradition, but it has no fixed public schedule and we don't promote or sell it; our buffalo fighting explainer sets out the facts. Monkeys trained to pick coconuts and elephant riding are other examples. We only work with animal experiences that don't involve riding, shows or bathing with elephants.

Experience Samui's culture

The easiest way into island culture is to see it with a local guide. The Jungle Discovery jeep safari (1,500 THB adult) visits temples, Wat Khunaram's mummified monk and the Secret Buddha Garden with no animal activities; our jungle safari guide compares the options.
